overview: Diaguita names encompass distinct communities and archaeological traditions on both sides of the Andes. The Chilean ceramic tradition and the peoples of Argentina’s Calchaquí valleys are related topics, not one uniform empire. The broad imported outline and its 1492 to 1500 dates should not imply a single government or historical lifetime.

periods.title: Regional farming societies
periods.summary: In Chile’s Norte Chico, Diaguita communities developed distinctive ceramics and settlements including El Olivar.

periods.title: Inca connections
periods.summary: Inca-period vessels combine Diaguita designs with imperial forms and other local traditions.

periods.title: Colonial resistance and dispossession
periods.summary: Spanish conquest proceeded unevenly; Kilmes families suffered forced removal in the seventeenth century.

periods.title: Continuing communities
periods.summary: Diaguita communities in Chile and Argentina continue farming, organizing and defending their identities.

items.text: In northwestern Argentina, peoples including the Quilmes and Tolombones maintained their own settlements and leaders. Their shared Diaguita designation can obscure that political variety. Communities cooperated and competed within a landscape of valleys, mountain slopes and valuable resources.

Mountain farming required creating usable ground. Diaguita farmers built low stone retaining walls and filled behind them to form terraces. Water channels and reservoirs helped direct scarce water toward crops. A sloping hillside could become a series of workable growing surfaces.

In Chile’s Norte Chico, irrigation supported maize, beans, quinoa and squash, while coastal resources supplied fish and shellfish. The museum also describes seagoing rafts with inflated sea-lion-skin floats. Valleys and ocean contributed different things to household livelihoods.

Modern Huasco Alto families grow crops and fruit near valley homes, while goat herds use more distant seasonal pastures. These living practices have their own colonial and later history. The goats and orchards must not be casually placed in a scene from 1492.

El Olivar near La Serena preserves houses, burial areas and rubbish deposits from successive communities. Large excavations followed discoveries during road construction in 2014. Carefully recording discarded material and its location helps reconstruct everyday activity alongside more spectacular objects.

The site also exposes a scholarly disagreement. Francisco Cornely used pottery changes to build a chronological sequence; Mary Shepherd Slusser emphasized stylistic unity in material from 63 excavated graves. Recent investigations have renewed interest in her interpretation.

A double kero cup in La Serena’s collection came from El Olivar’s FUN 8 area during the 2016 rescue excavation. The catalogue identifies it as Diaguita-Inca. Its documented recovery connects an unusual vessel with a particular archaeological context.

Another El Olivar vessel is a shoe-shaped jar with human features, recorded as inventory 72 and excavated by Cornely in sector R. Its memorable shape shows how potters combined containers with representations of people. The nickname describes its form, not footwear.

A vessel found in the Mapocho valley combines an Inca maka form, Diaguita decoration and materials associated with Aconcagua pottery. Museum curators suggest local artisans made it within those overlapping connections. They interpret it as probably holding maize beer, rather than claiming its contents were directly preserved.

The early Kakán dictionary described by the museum is lost, so it cannot supply a trustworthy quoted sentence here. A documented modern voice is leader Dora Clarisa Suárez’s Spanish “acá estamos”, meaning “here we are”. Her words assert the presence of Fuerte Alto’s Diaguita-Calchaquí community.

After defeat in 1665, Kilmes families were forced to leave their Calchaquí homeland and travel over 1,000 kilometers to the Río de la Plata. A colonial settlement was established in 1666. This traumatic removal concerns a particular people, not a single ending for every Diaguita community.

During pandemic school closures, an Amaicha del Valle teacher worked with community authorities to teach through local radio. Broadcasts reached children in distant places. The community’s council and leadership helped adapt a familiar technology to keep education going.

ending.text: Inca expansion and Spanish colonial campaigns altered sovereignty at different times across this region. Some communities faced forced relocation, while others followed different trajectories. Diaguita peoples continue in Chile and Argentina; the map’s 1500 endpoint does not date their disappearance.
